title: Give Responsibility for Disruptive Technologies to Organizations Whose Customers Need Them
hook: The team that owns the new initiative serves customers who do not need it. That is not a leadership problem. It is a placement problem.
counterintuition: The instinct is to place a disruptive effort where the relevant technical expertise lives. The problem is that technical expertise and customer pull are rarely in the same place. In fact, placement determines whose urgency governs the effort, and urgency follows customers, not capabilities.
tryThisNow: Name one new initiative in your organization and identify the team that currently owns it. Write down who that team's three most important customers are. Then write one sentence about whether those customers create pull toward or away from the initiative.
keyTakeaway: A unit prioritizes what its customers reward. Place a disruptive effort where those customers don't pull for it, and it will always lose. Placement determines which customers generate urgency.

breakdown.fastRead:
Organizational units protect what their customers value. A budget meeting inside a corporate banking division is governed by corporate banking customers: their compliance needs, their service expectations, their renewal risks. An initiative that does not serve those customers is an initiative that appears on nobody's urgent list. Strong executive backing does not change this. Executive backing does not generate the daily urgency that customer need generates.

Placing a disruptive effort with the right team is not about finding the best technical home. It is about finding the home whose customers will pull the effort forward. A telemedicine program placed inside the inpatient unit fails not because the technology is wrong or the team is uncommitted, but because inpatients do not need what the technology offers. The right customers are in a different unit.

Placement determines which customers are in the room.
breakdown.deepRead:
Priority-setting in an organizational unit follows customer signals. The customers that generate revenue, require service, and determine renewal decide what work feels urgent. The unit will allocate resources, people, and management attention toward work that those customers reward. Work that those customers do not reward will be deprioritized, scaled back, or absorbed into whatever higher-priority project is running at the time. This is not a failure of will. It is how organizations respond to the incentive environment their customers create. When a disruptive effort lands inside a unit whose customers have no stake in it, the effort is competing against the full weight of that customer environment.

Customer pull is not created by mandate. It is created by placement.

The correction is conceptually simple and organizationally hard. Find the unit whose customers would actually benefit from the disruptive effort. Those customers create the urgency that makes the initiative visible in priority-setting meetings. Without that pull, an initiative can have executive sponsorship, dedicated resources, and clear goals, and still fail to compete for the one thing development requires: consistent, uninterrupted attention.

The most common mistake is treating technical fit as a proxy for customer fit. A product that belongs technically inside the actuarial division may belong organizationally inside the direct-to-consumer team whose customers send weekly behavioral data. The actuarial expertise is an input. The customer pull is the environment the effort needs to survive.
breakdown.fullRead:
Think about the last time a new initiative at your organization was prioritized in a resource allocation meeting. What made it urgent? Most of the time urgency comes from a customer. A key account asked for the capability. A segment is threatening to go elsewhere. A partner flagged a delivery risk. The urgency is real and it is generated by a specific customer relationship. Initiatives that are not connected to any of those customer relationships are the ones that get moved to next quarter, then to the quarter after that, until the window that keeps not arriving becomes a quiet cancellation.

This is the placement problem in its most direct form. An initiative housed in a unit whose customers don't generate pull toward it will wait. It will wait for a window in the schedule that arrives only when the customers the unit actually serves have nothing pressing. In practice, customers who fund a unit's legitimacy always have something pressing. The window does not come. What executive backing can do is maintain the initiative on the agenda. What it cannot do is generate the day-to-day urgency that customer need generates.

The organizational logic is simple enough to see once it is named. Each unit serves a customer base. That customer base sets the standard for what matters. An initiative that serves a different customer base brings different needs into the unit, needs that the unit's customers do not share. Those needs feel like overhead rather than priority. They are not treated as overhead because anyone is obstructionist. They are treated as overhead because the customers generating urgency are telling the unit to focus elsewhere.

Julien's streaming studio showed this clearly. The cable programming division's customers were cable operators measuring success by subscriber count and content fill rates. The streaming platform required content measured by engagement duration and platform retention. Those were not metrics any cable operator was asking for. Every editorial decision drifted back toward what cable operators rewarded, because those were the customers whose signals reached the priority-setting process. The streaming studio did not fail to innovate. It responded to the customer environment inside the unit that owned it.

Laura's telemedicine program had the same structure. The inpatient unit held the technical infrastructure. Admitted patients were not candidates for remote follow-up. The urgent-care division down the hall served walk-in patients who preferred not to return in person for routine visits. Those patients never generated a single urgency signal inside the inpatient unit's planning process. The program stalled, not because anyone decided to stall it, but because the customers who could have sustained it were in a different unit.

Finding the right placement means asking a question before asking about technical fit or budget: whose customers would pull toward this effort if it were placed in their unit? That question points to where the initiative belongs. Technical expertise can be transferred. Customer pull cannot be manufactured. The unit whose customers generate pull toward the disruptive effort is the unit that will protect the initiative when priority trade-offs arrive.

An organizational unit will protect what its customers need. If the disruptive effort is not something those customers need, it will be protected by no one.

examples.title: Laura's Telemedicine Kiosk Waits in the Wrong Corridor

planSpec.domain: hospital system placing a telemedicine program inside the inpatient unit versus the urgent-care division
planSpec.audience: a hospital operations director deciding where to house a telemedicine pilot for non-emergency follow-up visits
planSpec.stakes: the inpatient unit's customers are admitted patients who don't need telemedicine; the urgent-care division sees walk-in patients who might prefer remote follow-up
planSpec.requiredBeat: Laura places the telemedicine pilot inside the inpatient unit because the technical infrastructure is there. Eighteen months later the pilot has produced nothing because no admitted patient needs what it offers.
mustInclude: the eighteen-month result from wrong placement
mustAvoid: implying that telemedicine is inherently better than in-person care

examples.scenario: The telemedicine kiosk stands at the end of the inpatient corridor, screen lit and camera mounted, with a sign-in prompt no one has opened. Laura placed the pilot here because the hospital's technical infrastructure and nursing coordination team are in this wing. The inpatient unit's admitted patients are not candidates for remote follow-up. The urgent-care division two floors down sees walk-in patients who would rather not return in person for a ten-minute check-in. No one in that division was part of the placement decision. Eighteen months after launch, the kiosk usage log shows eleven sessions.
examples.whatToDo: Before finalizing placement, identify which patient population the telemedicine format serves and whether those patients are in the inpatient unit. Technical infrastructure can be shared or moved. Customer pull cannot.
examples.whyItMatters: A telemedicine program placed inside a unit whose patients don't need it has no source of customer urgency. Without urgency, the program waits for a priority window that does not open.

examples.title: Ryan's P2P Roadmap Looks Exactly Like Corporate Banking Needs

planSpec.domain: retail bank housing its mobile peer-to-peer payment product inside the corporate banking division
planSpec.audience: a product director who placed the mobile payment product under corporate banking because the technical compliance team is there
planSpec.stakes: corporate banking customers have no need for P2P payment features; retail checking customers do, and they are in a different division
planSpec.requiredBeat: Ryan's product roadmap is shaped entirely by corporate banking requirements because those are the customers who fund the division's decisions. The retail checking customers who would use P2P daily are in a division that doesn't control the roadmap.
mustInclude: corporate compliance requirements dominating the roadmap
the structural explanation for why this happened
mustAvoid: suggesting that compliance requirements are unimportant

examples.scenario: Looking back at the mobile P2P product's roadmap, Ryan can trace where each priority came from. Every compliance checkpoint, every API security audit, every institutional transfer specification was a response to a corporate banking customer request. The retail checking customers who would use P2P daily to split bills and transfer small sums are in a different division with a different budget cycle. The retail division was never in the room when the roadmap was approved. The roadmap it produced looks exactly like what corporate banking customers needed and nothing like what retail customers do.
examples.whatToDo: Map roadmap decisions back to which customer base requested them before the next planning cycle. If the retail checking customers who need P2P are not generating roadmap inputs, move the product to the division whose customers will.
examples.whyItMatters: A product roadmap reflects the customers whose signals reach the team building it. If those customers are not the product's target users, the roadmap will serve the wrong customer base regardless of intent.

examples.title: Julien's Brief Arrives Listing Cable Subscribers as the Audience

planSpec.domain: broadcast media company housing its streaming studio inside the cable programming division
planSpec.audience: a content strategy director whose streaming studio budget is approved by cable programming executives whose renewal metrics are based on cable subscriber counts
planSpec.stakes: the cable programming division's customers are cable operators, not streaming subscribers — so the streaming studio keeps being asked to produce content that looks good on cable metrics
planSpec.requiredBeat: Julien has to decide whether to produce a streaming-native format that will perform poorly on cable metrics or adapt it to cable's needs and lose the streaming advantage. The decision is structurally forced by which division controls the budget and who their customers are.
mustInclude: cable operator as customer of the division
mustAvoid: treating cable vs. streaming as a technology battle rather than an organizational placement problem

examples.scenario: At 10:30 a.m., Julien opens the content brief for the streaming studio's first original series. The cable programming division has approved the project. The brief's target audience is listed as cable subscribers, because that is the metric the division's performance review tracks. Julien must decide whether to produce the series for cable engagement metrics, which will satisfy the division's customers, or for streaming platform metrics, which have no advocate in the budget process. The decision is not primarily about content quality. It is about which customer base is in the room.
examples.whatToDo: Before producing streaming-native content, identify whether the streaming platform's audience has representation in the division's priority-setting process. If not, the studio needs a different organizational home.
examples.whyItMatters: A streaming studio inside a cable division will produce content shaped by cable customers because those are the signals that reach the budget process. Organizational placement determines output, not technology.

examples.title: Astrid Predicts Two Years and Gets Two Actuarial Cycles

planSpec.domain: commercial insurer housing its usage-based insurance product inside the actuarial division
planSpec.audience: a product innovation director whose usage-based product sits inside actuarial because that's where the pricing models live
planSpec.stakes: actuarial's customers are underwriters who work on annual review cycles; the usage-based product requires weekly behavioral data from drivers
planSpec.requiredBeat: Astrid predicts the usage-based product will be ready for market in two years based on actuarial's modeling timeline. The reveal shows the product's iteration count matched the actuarial cycle, not the driver experience that should have shaped it.
mustInclude: the absence of driver-customer pull inside the actuarial division
mustAvoid: implying that actuarial modeling is wrong or outdated in general

examples.scenario: Which customers define success in an actuarial division? Underwriters who submit one annual policy review. Astrid's usage-based product needs weekly behavioral data from drivers to function. The actuarial division's cycle was built around the underwriter's annual timeline. The usage-based product is reviewed at the same cadence. Driver feedback is collected once a year. Astrid predicts the product will be market-ready in two years. Two years later, the product's iteration count matches the actuarial review cycle. The driver experience that should have shaped the weekly feedback loop was never in the room.
examples.whatToDo: Before placing the product inside actuarial, identify whether drivers are a customer the division has any process for. Pricing expertise can be accessed without the product living inside actuarial's priority and review cycle.
examples.whyItMatters: A product that needs weekly driver feedback placed inside a division built for annual review cycles will follow the annual cadence. The cadence is not a choice. It is the rhythm the unit's customers require.

examples.title: Luca's Subscription Box Is Curated for the Wrong Customer

planSpec.domain: legacy retailer housing its subscription box service inside the merchandising department
planSpec.audience: a merchandising director whose customers are wholesale buyers and store planners, not end consumers ordering personal curated boxes
planSpec.stakes: merchandising's planning cycles are seasonal and bulk-volume; subscription box requires weekly curation and individual-level personalization
planSpec.requiredBeat: Luca's postmortem on the failed subscription box pilot finds that the box was curated using wholesale buyer feedback. The individual subscriber's preference data was never in the room.
mustInclude: wholesale buyer feedback as the only signal
the postmortem finding the root cause in organizational placement
mustAvoid: treating subscription boxes as inherently harder than traditional retail

examples.scenario: The packing station is set up for bulk wholesale orders, twelve deep and uniform. Beside it, a subscription box sits waiting for curation notes from last Tuesday's wholesale buyer session. Luca's merchandising team knows how to collect wholesale buyer data. Individual subscriber preferences are tracked on a consumer app the team does not access. The subscription box is curated using the data the team knows how to use. Six months in, the boxes reflect wholesale buyer taste, not the preferences of the subscribers receiving them.
examples.whatToDo: Identify where subscriber preference data is held and whether the merchandising team can access it. Curation follows available customer signals. If those signals come from wholesale buyers, the subscription box will serve wholesale buyers.
examples.whyItMatters: A team curates using the customer signals it has access to. If the only accessible signal comes from wholesale buyers, the subscription box serves wholesale buyers. The subscriber's preference is not in the room.

examples.title: Min's On-Demand Jobs Run in the Gaps Between Offset Runs

planSpec.domain: commercial printing company housing its on-demand digital printing service inside the offset plant management team
planSpec.audience: a plant manager whose performance is measured by offset press utilization and long-run job efficiency
planSpec.stakes: on-demand digital printing thrives on short-run variety; the plant manager's incentives push toward long-run standardization
planSpec.requiredBeat: Before: Min's on-demand service is scheduled around offset press priority. After: the on-demand service is moved under the customer accounts team whose clients need quick turnaround, and scheduling is pulled by customer delivery dates rather than press utilization.
mustInclude: offset utilization metric as the scheduling driver
customer delivery date as the alternative driver
the explicit before/after in scheduling logic
mustAvoid: suggesting that offset printing is obsolete or that digital printing is always preferable

examples.scenario: You are reviewing the on-demand printing schedule from last month. Every on-demand job ran in the gap between offset press runs. Before: Min's on-demand service is inside the offset plant team whose metric is press utilization. On-demand jobs fill in around offset priority. After: the service moves to the customer accounts team. Customer delivery dates now set the schedule. On-demand jobs run when customers need them, not when the offset presses have space.
examples.whatToDo: Move on-demand scheduling authority to the team whose customers set the delivery dates. Press utilization metrics are correct for the offset team. On-demand scheduling needs to be pulled by a different customer's requirements.
examples.whyItMatters: A schedule governed by press utilization will always fit on-demand jobs around offset priority. Moving scheduling authority to the customer accounts team changes which customer requirements govern the daily plan.

questions.prompt: What determines which work an organizational unit treats as urgent?
choices: The executive strategy that the unit's leadership announces each quarter.
The size of the unit's allocated budget for new initiatives.
The needs of the customers that generate revenue and fund the unit's legitimacy.
questions.explanation: Customer need generates urgency. An organizational unit will protect and prioritize work that its customers reward. Work that those customers do not reward competes against an urgency it cannot match.

questions.prompt: A hospital operations director places a telemedicine pilot inside the inpatient unit because the technical infrastructure is there. Eighteen months later the pilot has stalled. What is the most likely structural explanation?
choices: Inpatient customers are admitted patients who don't need telemedicine. No customer pull existed inside the unit that owned the effort.
The inpatient unit lacked the technical competence to operate the telemedicine system.
The hospital's executive team did not provide sufficient budget support.
questions.explanation: Placement inside the inpatient unit gave the effort access to technical resources but disconnected it from customers who would use telemedicine. Without customer pull, the effort had no source of urgency inside its host organization.

questions.prompt: A retail bank places its mobile P2P payment product inside the corporate banking division because the compliance team is there. Retail checking customers who would use P2P daily are in a different division. What will the product's roadmap look like after one year?
choices: The roadmap will reflect both corporate and retail customer needs equally.
The roadmap will be shaped by corporate banking compliance requirements, because those are the customers funding the division's priority-setting.
The roadmap will stall because P2P payment is not technically feasible inside a corporate banking infrastructure.
questions.explanation: A division allocates its roadmap according to the needs of its customers. Corporate banking customers generate compliance requirements. Retail P2P customers generate user experience needs. The division whose customers are corporate banking will produce a compliance-shaped roadmap regardless of intent.

questions.prompt: A streaming studio is housed inside a cable programming division. Cable operators are the division's customers. Streaming subscribers are not. Which outcome best predicts what content the studio will produce over time?
choices: The studio will produce content optimized equally for cable and streaming audiences.
The studio will produce purely streaming-native content because streaming is the stated strategic priority.
The studio will produce content shaped by cable operator metrics because those are the customers whose signals reach the priority-setting process.
questions.explanation: The division's customers are cable operators. Cable operators reward cable performance metrics. The streaming studio lives inside the division's resource allocation and priority-setting system. Over time, customer signals from cable operators will shape the studio's output even if that is not the stated intent.

questions.prompt: A legacy retailer's subscription box pilot is housed inside the merchandising department. Merchandising's customers are wholesale buyers and store planners. Individual subscriber preferences are the signal the subscription box needs. Which result is most likely after two years?
choices: The subscription box will be curated using wholesale buyer feedback because that is the only customer signal the merchandising team knows how to collect and act on.
The subscription box will build a strong individual subscriber data set because the merchandising team is motivated to make it succeed.
The subscription box will develop its own subscriber feedback system independently of the merchandising team's existing processes.
questions.explanation: The merchandising team knows how to collect and respond to wholesale buyer feedback. That is the customer input their processes are built around. An initiative inside that unit will be served by those processes, not by subscriber-level feedback the unit has no system to collect.

questions.prompt: Why does executive backing for a disruptive initiative fail to substitute for customer pull?
choices: Because executives are often not trusted by frontline teams in most organizations, which limits how far their backing can travel below senior leadership.

Because executive backing sets the agenda but does not generate the day-to-day urgency that customer need creates. The priority signals that determine actual resource allocation come from customers, not from executive support.
Because executives lack the technical authority to override a unit's existing priorities and cannot direct resources below the level of their direct reports.
questions.explanation: Executive sponsorship can keep an initiative visible and funded at a nominal level. What it cannot do is generate the persistent urgency that customer need generates daily. Urgency determines what gets consistent attention. Customer pull determines urgency. Placement determines which customers produce that pull.

questions.prompt: A plant manager's on-demand digital printing service is housed inside the offset plant team. The offset team's performance is measured by press utilization and long-run job efficiency. What will happen to on-demand job scheduling over time?
choices: On-demand jobs will be scheduled according to customer delivery dates because that is what the customers need.
On-demand and offset jobs will be scheduled according to a neutral priority system that serves both equally.
On-demand jobs will be scheduled around offset press priority because the metrics that govern the team's performance are offset utilization metrics.
questions.explanation: A team's scheduling decisions follow its performance metrics. If the metrics reward offset utilization, the team will protect offset utilization. On-demand jobs will fill the gaps rather than set the schedule. This is not obstruction. It is the team optimizing for what it is measured on.

questions.prompt: An insurer's usage-based product is housed inside the actuarial division. Actuarial customers are underwriters who work on annual review cycles. The usage-based product requires weekly behavioral data from drivers. What does the actuarial division's review cycle reveal about the product's development pace?
choices: The actuarial review cycle will govern the product's iteration rhythm because the division's processes were built for its customers, not for weekly driver feedback loops.
The usage-based product will force the actuarial division to adopt a weekly iteration cycle because that is what the product requires.
The product will stall entirely because actuarial expertise is irrelevant to usage-based products.
questions.explanation: An organizational unit's processes are built for the customers it serves. Actuarial processes are built around annual review cycles because underwriters work on annual timelines. Placing a product that needs weekly driver feedback inside a unit built for annual cycles means the product will follow the actuarial cadence, not create a new one.

questions.prompt: A company argues that customer-fit placement is less important than strong executive commitment because a committed executive can override any structural constraint. How should this argument be assessed?
choices: The argument is correct: committed executives with sufficient organizational authority can override any structural constraint if they apply consistent attention and are willing to reassign resources.

Executive commitment can maintain nominal support for an initiative but cannot replace the day-to-day urgency that comes from serving customers who actually need the effort. Structure generates persistent urgency. Executive commitment does not.
Executive commitment is irrelevant: only organizational structure and resource allocation authority determine what gets prioritized over time.
questions.explanation: Executive support matters but is not sufficient. An executive can keep an initiative alive, funded, and on the agenda. What generates the consistent priority that development requires is customer pull: the daily signal from customers who need what the initiative offers. Without that signal, the effort competes for attention that customer-serving work will always need more urgently.

reviewCards.front: A new initiative keeps losing priority in resource allocation despite executive support. What structural explanation should you investigate first?
reviewCards.back: Investigate whether the team that owns the initiative serves customers who actually need what it offers. If those customers don't generate pull toward the initiative, executive support cannot substitute for the urgency customer need creates.

reviewCards.front: What does 'customer pull' mean in the context of organizational placement?
reviewCards.back: Customer pull is the urgency generated when an organizational unit's customers need what an initiative offers. Initiatives with customer pull inside their host unit are protected and prioritized. Initiatives without it compete against work that customers are actively rewarding.

reviewCards.front: An initiative is placed inside a unit with strong technical expertise but the wrong customers. What happens over time?
reviewCards.back: The initiative's roadmap, scheduling, and priority-setting drift toward the needs of the unit's actual customers. Technical fit cannot substitute for customer fit. Placement determines which customers generate urgency.

reviewCards.front: You are choosing between two teams to own a disruptive initiative. One has technical expertise; the other's customers would actively pull toward it. Which placement factor matters most?
reviewCards.back: Whose customers would pull toward this initiative if it were placed in their unit? Not: which team has the most relevant technical expertise. Customer pull must come from within the host organization's customer base.

reviewCards.front: Why does an initiative's priority-setting problem look like a leadership problem rather than a placement problem?
reviewCards.back: Because the individual decisions that deprioritize the initiative are defensible on their own terms. Each scheduling conflict or budget revision is local. The cumulative effect of wrong placement shows up slowly, as a pattern.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to diagnose whether an initiative is placed inside a unit whose customers generate pull toward it, and to distinguish customer-fit placement from technical-fit placement when choosing where a disruptive effort belongs.

ifThenPlans.context: a new initiative is repeatedly deprioritized despite executive backing
ifThenPlans.plan: If the initiative keeps losing in resource allocation, then identify whose customers are generating urgency inside the owning unit and whether those customers have any need for what the initiative offers. The problem may be placement, not commitment.

ifThenPlans.context: deciding where to house a new disruptive initiative
ifThenPlans.plan: If you are choosing which team owns the initiative, then map each candidate team's three most important customers and ask which of those customer sets would generate pull toward the initiative before considering technical expertise.

ifThenPlans.context: reviewing a disruptive initiative's roadmap and finding it shaped by the wrong requirements
ifThenPlans.plan: If the roadmap reflects the host unit's customers rather than the initiative's target customers, then treat the roadmap drift as a placement signal: the initiative is inside the wrong organizational home.

ifThenPlans.context: evaluating whether an initiative needs a separate team or can stay inside an existing unit
ifThenPlans.plan: If the initiative's target customers differ significantly from the owning unit's current customers, then assess whether those target customers can generate urgency inside the existing unit or whether separation is needed to give the initiative a customer base of its own.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Name one new initiative in your organization and identify the team that currently owns it. Write down who that team's three most important customers are. Then write one sentence about whether those customers create pull toward or away from the initiative.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, when sitting in a priority-setting or resource allocation meeting, identify which customer sent the signal that made one initiative urgent and which initiatives lost priority because no customer was pulling for them.

memorableLines.text: Placement determines which customers are in the room.
memorableLines.why: Converts the entire placement argument into one concrete, verifiable claim.

memorableLines.text: Customer pull is not created by mandate. It is created by placement.
memorableLines.why: Names the exact thing executive backing cannot substitute for, in two sentences.

memorableLines.text: An organizational unit will protect what its customers need. If the disruptive effort is not something those customers need, it will be protected by no one.
memorableLines.why: States the consequence of wrong placement directly without hedging.
